sections.h2: Who assesses and who collects in Racine
sections.html:
Racine splits the work between two governments. The City Assessor Division sets your assessed value. The city itself takes tax payments through July 31, and the Racine County Treasurer collects whatever is still unpaid after that date. The city sits on Lake Michigan at the Root River mouth, 22 miles south of Milwaukee and 60 miles north of Chicago, and had 77,816 residents in the 2020 census. ZIP codes run from 53401 to 53408.

The Assessor Division works from City Hall, 730 Washington Avenue, Room 308. It holds the parcel legal descriptions, ownership records, property and sales data, and the assessment rolls. Questions can start at cityofracinewi.gov. For looking up what a given parcel owes, the county's Ascent Land Records tax search is the tool most owners use.

Racine owners may pay in four parts. Every one of the four goes to the city, and bills are mailed in December. City payment questions go to (262) 636-9171.

Racine installment schedule
Due dateWhere to pay
January 31City of Racine
March 31City of Racine
May 31City of Racine
July 31City of Racine
After July 31Racine County Treasurer, 730 Wisconsin Ave

Most of the rest of the county has two dates, not four. If you close in spring, you may be selling a house with two city payments still open, so settle who pays them in the contract.

Miss a date, or pay less than the amount due, and the whole balance for the year comes due together. The four-part option ends. Interest and penalties begin February 1 under Wis. Stat. ss. 74.11(7) and 74.12(7), at a combined 1.5 percent per month under s. 74.47. The county treasurer has no room to adjust those charges.

  • Even a small shortfall on one installment has the same effect as skipping it.
  • After July 31 the leftover balance is payable to the county treasurer instead of the city.
  • The county invites owners with back taxes to arrange regular payments and takes them.

Before a sale closes, ask both offices for a year-by-year figure. The current year can be open with the city while an older year sits with the county.

State law requires assessment at market value. The Assessor Division defines that as the price a typical, well-informed buyer would pay with no pressure on either side. The assessor reads the market and does not invent a value. A revaluation is a full review of all assessments so they stay even across the city.

The division names the changes that usually push a value up: extra rooms or a garage, new siding, a substantially updated kitchen or bath, central air and extensive remodeling. Law calls for valuing from an actual view or the best information available, and the division says seeing inside and out works best. If an owner refuses an interior inspection, the assessor uses the exterior and sales of comparable homes. Owners must be notified whenever an assessment changes.

The path runs through open book and then the Board of Review. Each year the city sets an open book window in Room 308 and a Board of Review date, so ask the Assessor Division for the current schedule. By the time the bill shows up in December it is too late to object, and paying under protest counts only if you first filed with the board.

  • Give notice of intent to object at least 48 hours before the first board meeting, unless you show good cause during the first two hours of that meeting (s. 70.47(7)(a)).
  • File the written objection during those two hours and challenge the combined value of land and improvements.
  • Expect to be sworn in. The assessor has to attend the first meeting.
  • The clerk posts notice at least 15 days ahead, or 30 days in a revaluation year.

sections.h2: After the sale: ownership and forms
sections.html:
The new owner's name reaches the tax bill through the Assessor's Office about two weeks after the deed is recorded with the Register of Deeds. Owner data for bills is normally pulled from the city's database in November, so a house sold between mid-November and December may still show the old owner on that year's bill. Call the Assessor's Office for the latest.

The division also handles a change of address form, available in Room 308, which needs an agent authorization form when someone files for another person. Combining or splitting contiguous parcels you own uses a separate form. Name changes are recorded with the Register of Deeds, where a recorded survey can also be found, at (262) 636-3208, 730 Wisconsin Avenue.

Exemption requests are due at the Assessor's Office by March 1 to count for the current assessment year.

The lottery and gaming credit shows up as a reduction on a qualifying bill. Apply or remove it through the Department of Revenue's online portal, where late claims are due by October 1. The homestead credit is a different thing, claimed on your Wisconsin income tax return and aimed at lower-income households. The county treasurer explains both, and links a veteran's credit page too.

The Assessor page also links the state's Guide for Property Owners for 2026, which walks through assessment accuracy, tax procedures and yearly valuation updates.

Gather three numbers: current-year installments still owed to the city, any older balance held by the county treasurer, and the interest on both. The title company or closing attorney adds them to the payoff statement. A buyer who takes the house as is still gets a deed that must be recorded with the county, so clean tax records help the closing move.

If you inherited the house, tell the Assessor's Office once the deed is recorded so the bill goes out in the right name. If several years are delinquent, call the county treasurer about the foreclosure timeline before you list. The county sells foreclosed properties by sealed bid and over-the-counter sale, and a sale that closes first avoids that path.

A practical order of calls works well. Start with the Assessor Division in Room 308 to confirm the owner name and parcel details on record. Next phone the city at (262) 636-9171 for what is open for the current year. Then ask the county treasurer about anything older. Last, check with the Register of Deeds at (262) 636-3208 that the deed and any name change were recorded properly. Each office holds a different piece of the file, and a payoff that leaves one out can delay the closing.

faqs.q: Who gets my property tax payment in the City of Racine?
faqs.a: The city, on January 31, March 31, May 31 and July 31. From August 1 on, pay the Racine County Treasurer at 730 Wisconsin Avenue. Payment questions go to (262) 636-9171.

faqs.q: Can I pay in installments in Racine?
faqs.a: Yes. The city offers four, on January 31, March 31, May 31 and July 31. Most other places in Racine County offer two.

faqs.q: When does a new owner appear on a Racine tax bill?
faqs.a: About two weeks after the deed is recorded, the Assessor's Office updates ownership. Names for bills are normally pulled in November, so a mid-November or December sale may not show on that year's bill.

faqs.q: Where is the Racine Assessor's Office?
faqs.a: City Hall, 730 Washington Avenue, Room 308. It handles address changes, parcel splits and combines, and exemption requests, which are due March 1.

faqs.q: When does the Racine Board of Review meet?
faqs.a: The date is set each year. Call the Assessor Division for the open book and board schedule, and give notice 48 hours before the first meeting.
